With over 153 million people projected to be affected by AD by 2050 (Livingston et al. 20, the disease imposes an enormous socioeconomic burden on healthcare systems worldwide (Chen et al. Despite decades of research, there are currently limited treatment options for AD, and existing therapies provide only symptomatic relief without addressing the underlying neurodegenerative processes.

The pathological hallmarks of AD include extracellular amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, synaptic dysfunction, and chronic neuroinflammation (Cheng et al. 2015; Cho et al. 2022; Lee et al. These multifactorial features highlight the complexity of AD and underscore the need for novel therapeutic strategies that can target multiple aspects of the disease simultaneously (Ibrahim et al.2019; Maramai et al. 2020; Zhang et al.20.

One of the most well-studied mechanisms of AD pathology is the amyloid cascade hypothesis, which posits that abnormal accumulation of Aβ peptides initiates a cascade of events leading to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal death, and cognitive decline (Baek et al. 2017; Bae et al. 2020a, b; Han et al. Aβ peptides are generated from amyloid precursor protein (APP) through sequential cleavage by β-secretase (BACE and γ-secretase, resulting in the formation of toxic Aβ oligomers and plaques (Bahn et al. 2019; Park et al. 2021a, b; Hong et al. Although recent Aβ-targeting therapies have shown some promise, their effects have been limited, suggesting that reducing Aβ burden alone may be insufficient for halting disease progression.

Recent studies have indicated that neuroinflammatory processes, particularly those involving the NLRP3 inflammasome and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, also play a critical role in AD pathogenesis by exacerbating neuronal damage and amyloid deposition (Leng et al. 2021; Tang et al. This suggests that a multi-target approach that addresses both amyloid accumulation and neuroinflammation may offer a more effective therapeutic strategy.
Synaptic dysfunction is another prominent feature of AD, closely associated with cognitive impairment.
Synaptic integrity is maintained by complex molecular networks (Cho et al. 20 involving postsynaptic density proteins (e.g., PSD and presynaptic vesicle-associated proteins (e.g., synaptophysin).
Alterations in synaptic proteins, as well as mitochondrial dysfunction, contribute to impaired synaptic transmission and neuronal communication, Y. ultimately leading to cognitive deficits.

Given that synaptic health is fundamental to learning and memory, strategies that restore synaptic function may help improve cognitive outcomes in AD patients (Tzioras et al. In previous studies, we demonstrated that ramalin (γ-glutamyl-N′-(2-hydroxyphenyl)hydrazide), a natural compound isolated from the Antarctic lichen Ramalina terebrata, exerts potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial effects (Paudel et al. 2011; Kim et al. We synthesized ramalin with other functional groups to develop drugs that have enhanced therapeutic effects, reduced toxicity, increased permeability, or improved yields.
Among the compounds, (S)-4-amino-5,5-difluoro- N′-methyl-N′-phenylpentanehydrazide hydrochloride (RA- 058HM) exhibited low toxicity, high stability, potent brain diffusion, and high yields.
RA-058HM is a novel compound that shows promise in modulating multiple aspects of AD pathology.

In this study, we demonstrate that RA-058HM mitigates both amyloid and inflammatory pathways, potentially reducing Aβ plaque formation, restoring synaptic transmission, and alleviating neuroinflammation.

To evaluate its effects on cognitive performance, amyloid burden, synaptic function, and neuroinflammation, we used the 5xFAD mouse model—a wellestablished transgenic model of AD. The 5xFAD model, known for its accelerated Aβ deposition, synaptic loss, and cognitive decline, is particularly well-suited for studying the complex pathology of AD. Materials and methods Synthesis of t ert ‑bu tyl ‑(s )‑( 1,1 ‑di flu oro ‑5‑ (2‑ met hyl ‑2‑ phe nyl hyd raz ine yl) ‑5‑ oxopentan‑2‑yl)carbamate (RA‑058HM‑Boc) A 100 mL round-bottom flask equipped with a magnetic stir bar was charged with (S)-4-((tert-butoxycarbonyl)amino)- 5,5-difluoropentanoic acid (1.0 g, 3.95 mmol) dissolved in 20 mL of dichloromethane (DCM).
The reaction mixture was cooled to 0 ℃, and triethylamine (TEA, 1.2 equivalents, 4.74 mmol, 660 µL) was added dropwise.

After stirring for 10 min, ethyl chloroformate (ECF, 1.2 equivalents, 4.74 mmol, 451 µL) was added gradually over a period of 1 h. The reaction continued to stir at 0 ℃ for another 4 h. Separately, in a 50 mL pear-shaped flask, 1-methyl-1-phenylhydrazine (1.2 equivalents, 4.74 mmol, 579 mg) was dissolved in 10 mL of DCM. This solution was carefully introduced into the primary reaction mixture over one hour, maintaining a temperature of 0 ℃.

After completing the hydrazine addition, the reaction was warmed to room temperature and stirred for another 16 h. Upon completion, the organic layer was washed sequentially with distilled water, 1 A novel multi‑target compound mitigates amyloid plaques, synaptic deficits, N hydrochloric acid, 0.5 N sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO ), and then rinsed again with distilled water.
The organic phase was separated, dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate (Na SO ), and concentrated using a rotary evaporator.
The target product was purified through recrystallization from a mixture of ethyl acetate and n-hexane (1:5).
The yield of RA-058HM-Boc was 95%, resulting in 1.34 g of the product.

Synthesis of (S)‑4‑amino‑5,5‑difluoro‑N′‑meth yl‑N′‑phenylpentanehydrazide hydrochloride (RA‑058HM) A 250 mL round-bottom flask fitted with a magnetic stir bar was charged with RA-058HM-Boc (1.0 g, 2.80 mmol).

The compound was dissolved in 50 mL of 1 M hydrochloric acid (HCl) in ethyl acetate (EA, 50 mmol), and the reaction was allowed to proceed at room temperature (24 ℃) for approximately 18 h. Afterward, the resulting white solid was filtered and washed sequentially with EA and n-hexane.
The filtered solid was then dried under vacuum to yield the RA-058HM.
The yield of RA-058HM was 93%, resulting in 0.77 g of the product.

Microsomal stability The liver microsome stability test was initiated by adding RA-058HM (e.g., 1 μM, adjustable) or a positive control, along with the NADPH regenerating system, to human or animal plasma at 37 ℃.
The samples were incubated at 37 ℃ for a specified time (e.g., 0 and 30 min, adjustable).
After incubation, acetonitrile containing an internal standard was added, followed by centrifugation.
The supernatant was then injected into an LC–MS/MS system for analysis to determine the half-life (t ), percent remaining, and intrinsic clearance (n = 3).
The concentration of RA-058HM was quantified and compared to the 0-min time point.
The comparison values are expressed as a percentage of the remaining.
The Ln% of remaining values at each time point are used to calculate the elimination constant (k), from which the half-life (t ) (min) and intrinsic clearance (CL ) (μL·min−1·mg−1) are derived.

CYP drug metabolism enzyme inhibition evaluation (IC50 assay) Human liver microsomes, phosphate buffer (pH 7., each CYP substrate drug (CYP1A2; phenacetin, CYP2C9; diclofenac, CYP2C19; S-mephenytoin, CYP2D6; dextromethorphan, CYP3A; midazolam), and RA-058HM (e.g., 0, 10 μM, adjustable) were incubated at 37 ℃ for 20 min with the NADPH regenerating system.
After incubation, acetonitrile containing an internal standard was added to terminate the reaction.
After the reaction, the supernatant was analyzed by LC–MS/MS to assess the metabolic activity , and… 747 of each CYP enzyme based on the metabolites of the respective substrate drugs.
The system was validated using known CYP inhibitors (e.g., Ketoconazole for CYP3A) to assess the degree of enzyme inhibition.
The degree of metabolic enzyme inhibition by RA-058HM was expressed as the percentage of remaining activity compared to the control group (without RA-058HM).
Reverse mutation test (Ames test) The test was divided into two groups: with and without metabolic activation, and two plates were used for each dose.

For the non-metabolic activation group, 100 µL of each RA- 058HM, negative control, and positive control were added to tubes, followed by the addition of 500 µL of 0.1 mol/L phosphate buffer (pH 7. and 100 µL of bacterial suspension for each strain.
Then, 2 mL of Salmonella top agar was added to TA98, TA100, TA1535, and TA1537 strains, and 2 mL of E.coli top agar was added to WP2uvrA(pKM1 strain, followed by vortexing.
Afterward, the suspension was overlaid on minimal glucose agar plates and left at room temperature.
For the metabolic activation group, 500 µL of S9 mix was added instead of 500 µL of 0.1 mol/L phosphate buffer (pH 7., and the remaining procedures were performed in the same manner.

After the top agar solidified, the plates were inverted and incubated at 37 ℃ in a ThermoStableTM IF-55 incubator (DAIHAN-Sci, Republic of Korea) for 48 h. To investigate contamination by microorganisms, 100 µL of the highest dose of the RA-058HM, 500 µL of 0.1 mol/L phosphate buffer (pH 7., and 500 µL of S9 mix were added to tubes.
Top agar was then added, followed by vortexing, and the mixture was overlaid onto nutrient broth agar plates, which were left at room temperature.
After the top agar solidified, the plates were inverted and incubated at 37 ℃ for 24 h. The presence of colonies due to microbial contamination was counted.

Parallel artificial membrane permeability assay (PAMPA) The PAMPA-BBB model applied in this study was based on the BBB model described in the literature (Di et al. Conditions and P calculation of the PAMPA-BBB model were identical to the PAMPA-BLM model, except for the artificial lipid membrane used (Mensch et al. The lipid membrane of the PAMPA-BBB model was prepared by dissolving 20 mg of porcine polar brain lipid (PBL) in 1 mL of dodecane.
The filter membranes of the PAMPA- BBB model were coated with 4 μl of the porcine PBL solution.

With this setup of identical experimental conditions, the ability of both artificial lipid formulations (BLM vs. PBL) to provide the required BBB classification could be evaluated. 7 48 Radical scavenging assay The antioxidant activity of RA-058HM was evaluated using the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) free radical scavenging assay.
Stock solutions of RA-058HM were prepared at 1000 μg/mL in methanol.
From these stock solutions, serial dilutions of RA-058HM were prepared to final concentrations of 1, 2.5, 5, and 10 μM.
For each concentration, 1 mL of RA-058HM solution was mixed with 1 mL of a freshly prepared DPPH solution (0.002 g/mL in methanol).
An additional 1 mL of methanol was added to bring the final reaction volume to 3 mL. The blank control consisted of DPPH in methanol at a 1:2 ratio without any test compound.
All mixtures were incubated at room temperature (25 ℃) in the dark for 30 min to minimize light-induced degradation of DPPH.
After incubation, the absorbance of each sample was measured at 517 nm using a spectrophotometer.
The radical scavenging activity was calculated relative to the control.

Novel object recognition test The novel object recognition test (NORT) is widely used to assess cognitive function in mice (Leger et al. After administering RA-058HM, NORT was conducted as previously described, with minor modifications (Miedel et al. On the first day of the experiment, mice were placed in an open field (50 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm) and allowed to explore for 10 min to acclimate.

The following day, mice were placed in the same open field with two identical objects (familiar objects) and allowed to explore the objects for 10 min (training session). 3 h after a training session, one familiar object was replaced with a novel object.
Mice were then returned to the open field and allowed to explore the objects (test session).
During the test session, video recordings were made for subsequent analysis and review.

MWM was conducted as previously described with minor modifications (Park et al. A pool with a diameter of 120 cm was used for the test.

Mice were anaesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of Zoletil (Virbac) and Rompun (Bayer).
Following anesthesia, the mice were perfused with phosphate-buffered saline, and their brains were carefully extracted.
The brains were then divided into two hemispheres; one was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, while the other was dissected to separate the cortex and hippocampus.
The separated tissues were then snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80 ℃ until further biochemical analysis.
Western blot analysis Mouse brain tissues were homogenized with RIPA lysis buffer (Merck), mixed with protease/phosphatase inhibitor cocktail, and incubated for 30 min at 4 ℃.
After incubation, homogenized samples were centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 30 min at 4 ℃.
The supernatant was used for western blot (WB) as previously described (Bahn et al. Primary antibodies used for WB are listed in Table S1. β-Actin was used as the housekeeping gene.
Brain tissue frozen section Brain hemispheres preserved in 4% paraformaldehyde were sequentially soaked in 10%, 20%, and 30% sucrose (Junsei) in PBS solution for one day each at 4 ℃.
Tissues were then embedded in FSC 22 Frozen Section Media (Leica) and stored at −20 ℃.
Frozen samples were sectioned at a thickness of 30 μm using a cryotome (Leica) and stored in a cryoprotectant solution (Biosolution).

Thioflavin S staining Frozen sectioned brain slices were floated onto PBS and stained with 1% thioflavin S (Sigma) dissolved in 50% ethanol for 8 min. Stained samples were then washed with 80% ethanol and PBS. After washing, the samples were mounted onto slide glass with VECTASHIELD® Antifade Mounting Medium without DAPI (Vector Laboratories).

Results Synthesis and characterization of RA‑058HM The synthesis of the target compound tert-butyl-(S)-(1,1difluoro-5-(2-methyl-2-phenylhydrazineyl)-5-oxopentan- 2-yl)carbamate (RA-058HM-Boc) was achieved starting from (S)-4-((tert-butoxycarbonyl)amino)-5,5-difluoropentanoic acid (CAS No. The coupling reaction was performed according to the standard procedure used for ramalin derivatives, utilizing ethyl chloroformate (ECF) and triethylamine (TEA) under low-temperature conditions (0 ℃), as outlined in the materials and methods section.
This , and… 751 reaction yielded 95% of RA-058HM-Boc, which is notably higher than the typical 80–85% yield observed in the largescale syntheses of other ramalin derivatives.

This high yield may be attributed to the structural characteristics of the starting material, particularly the presence of difluoride groups, which likely facilitated a more efficient reaction process.
Following the synthesis of RA-058HM-Boc, the Boc (tert-butoxycarbonyl) group was removed under ambient conditions using 1 M hydrochloric acid in ethyl acetate (EA).
During the deprotection process, a crystalline precipitate formed, which was subsequently collected by filtration and washed with EA and n-hexane.
This method yielded the final product, (S)-4-amino-5,5-difluoro-N′-methyl-N′phenylpentanehydrazide hydrochloride (RA-058HM), with a yield of 93%.
The synthesized RA-058HM is a white crystalline HCl salt with good solubility in water.
Further solubility testing in water is planned to evaluate its properties comprehensively.

These structural features enable the achievement of higher yields of these ramalin derivatives compared to conventional outcomes, without altering the established synthetic methods (Fig. An inhibitory interaction potential test of RA-058HM on cytochrome P450 (CYP) was conducted with other ramalin compounds.
Mean control activities of 5 CYP isoforms were 95% or more, indicating no or weak inhibitory interaction (Table 1).
Metabolic stability tests using mouse, rat, dog, monkey, and human liver microsomes resulted in 90% or more of the remaining value, indicating a stable state of RA- 058HM (Table 2).

The toxicology test in vitro was confirmed by a reverse mutation test (Fig. 1B and C), and the in vivo study was conducted using ICR mice, with weight, blood, and spleen examinations (Fig. 1D, Table 3, and supplementary Fig. These data demonstrated the low toxicity of RA-058HM, which we selected as a drug candidate.

To assess whether RA-058HM could reach brain tissue, we conducted a parallel artificial membrane permeability assay (PAMPA), which indicated high blood–brain barrier permeability (Table 4), with a permeability coefficient (Pe) of 10.49 × 10−6 cm/sec. Although these results support CNS availability, we acknowledge that PAMPA reflects only passive diffusion and does not fully capture in vivo pharmacokinetics.

RA‑058HM ameliorates amyloidogenesis in the 5xFAD mice hippocampus Amyloid precursor protein (APP), a type 1 transmembrane glycoprotein, is sequentially cleaved by β-secretase and γ-secretase to generate amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides, particularly the neurotoxic Aβ isoform.
Aβ monomers then undergo nucleation, secondary growth, and elongation processes, , and… 755 forming oligomers that eventually aggregate into fibrils, which in turn form amyloid plaques.
To investigate the impact of RA-058HM on amyloidogenesis, we performed Western blot analysis, qPCR, and immunohistochemistry.
Western blot results showed a significant reduction in human APP (hAPP) protein levels in the hippocampus of 7-month-old 5xFAD mice treated with RA-058HM compared to vehicle-treated controls.

Additionally, both levels of protein and RNA of BACE1, the key β-secretase responsible for initiating Aβ formation, were reduced in the hippocampus of RA-058HM-treated 5xFAD mice compared to vehicle-treated controls (Fig. Notably, there was no significant change in BACE1 levels in the cortex (Fig. To further assess amyloid pathology, we performed Thioflavin S staining to visualize senile plaques (Fig. Quantification revealed a significant reduction in plaque density in the hippocampus of RA-058HM-treated 5xFAD mice compared to vehicle-treated controls (Fig. Also, we observed substantial decreases in soluble Aβ forms in RA-058HM-treated 5xFAD mice compared to vehicletreated 5xFAD controls, in both the hippocampus and cortex (Supplementary Fig. These findings indicate that RA-058HM effectively reduces amyloidogenesis in the hippocampus of 5xFAD mice, suggesting a potential therapeutic mechanism for ameliorating AD pathology.
RA‑058HM restores synaptic transmission function in 5xFAD hippocampal neurons Synapses are critical sites where neurons transfer signals, communicate, and influence brain function.

Neural activity can modify various brain processes by regulating synaptic transmission (Citri et al. To assess synaptic function, specifically synaptic transmission, we used a pHluorin-based assay, which involves pHluorin conjugated to the luminal region of synaptic vesicle membrane proteins such as vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (vGlut1, vG-pH).

RA-058HM (5 μM) was administered to hippocampal neurons derived from 5xFAD mice, and these 5xFAD hippocampal neurons expressing vG-pH were stimulated with 100 action potentials (APs) at 10 Hz. Fluorescence intensity was then measured to quantify synaptic transmission.
In WT neurons, the average synaptic transmission following 100 APs was approximately 20%.
In contrast, synaptic transmission in 5xFAD neurons was significantly impaired, dropping to around 11%.

RA‑058HM relieves neuroinflammation in 5xFAD hippocampus To determine whether RA-058HM alleviates neuroinflammation in the AD model, we conducted Western blot and qPCR analysis of various inflammatory markers.

Numerous therapeutic approaches have been explored for AD, with the ultimate goal of restoring or preventing cognitive deficits.

Among the pathological hallmarks of AD, amyloid plaques—derived from the amyloid precursor protein (APP)—are considered highly neurotoxic.
BACE1 plays a crucial role in the amyloidogenic pathway by initiating the conversion of APP into the amyloid-beta (Aβ ) monomer, which subsequently aggregates to form plaques.

Aberrant upregulation of this pathway is a consistent pathological feature of AD (Jo et al. 2010; Gwon et al. 2012; Cheng et al. Treatment with RA-058HM resulted in the downregulation of both amyloid plaques and BACE1 expression, suggesting a direct or indirect modulation of the amyloidogenic cascade.
This attenuation of amyloid pathology may alleviate neuronal toxicity and facilitate the restoration of neuronal function, while also reducing inflammation.
Key observations include the restoration of mitochondrial motility and a reduction in oxidative stress.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired trafficking are well-documented features of AD pathology (Baek et al. 2017; Han et al. 20, contributing to energy deficits and exacerbating neuronal damage.
These findings suggest that RA-058HM may improve cellular energy homeostasis by enhancing mitochondrial motility and reducing oxidative stress, thereby supporting the energy demands of synapses.
This mechanism is consistent with the observed restoration of synaptic function and cognitive improvement.

This aspect of RA-058HM’s mechanism provides a promising avenue for future research, as enhancing mitochondrial health may be a complementary strategy to amyloid-targeted therapies in AD. Learning impairments in rodents are frequently associated with genetic and pharmacological disruption of multiple components of the NMDAR multiprotein complexes , and… 759 (NRC), including proteins such as NR1, NR2A, NR2B, PSD95, PKA subunits, PKC isoforms, CaMKII, PP1, PP2A, PP2B, MEK, NF1, nNOS, cPLA2 and L1 (Husi et al. In this study, we examined PSD95, a postsynaptic marker, and synaptophysin, a presynaptic marker to assess the integrity of synaptic structures in the AD model.
Although we anticipated a reduction in these synaptic markers due to AD pathology, no significant differences were observed between treated and untreated 5xFAD mice.

The maintenance of PSD95 and synaptophysin levels may be crucial for preserving baseline synaptic function, as maintaining homeostatic levels of synaptic proteins likely supports the structural and functional stability of synapses.

Further investigation into other components, such as ion channels, G-protein-coupled receptors, and SNARE proteins, would provide additional insights into how RA-058HM sustains synaptic function in the 5xFAD model.
Our findings also demonstrated that RA-058HM significantly reduced NLRP3 inflammasome levels, a core component in the formation and persistence of Aβ plaques.

The NLRP3 inflammasome, in conjunction with ASC and caspase-1, is a well-established driver of neuroinflammation in AD. By downregulating NLRP3, RA-058HM may reduce Aβ plaque formation or limit its pathological effects, thereby contributing to the observed improvements in cognitive function.

Interestingly, while IBA1 levels, a marker for microglial activation, did not differ significantly between the vehicle and RA-058HM-treated groups, the reduction in NLRP3 suggests a shift in microglial activation states rather than changes in cell numbers.
This could imply that while microglial numbers remain stable, RA-058HM alters their phenotype or functional state, possibly shifting them towards a less pro-inflammatory state.
This modulation of microglial activation warrants further investigation to clarify the drug’s impact on glial cell function and its downstream effects on neuronal health.

While our findings demonstrate that RA- 058HM reduces NLRP3 and NF-κB activation in microglial cells and alleviates multiple AD-related pathologies in vivo, the precise molecular targets of RA-058HM remain to be fully elucidated.

Future studies will be needed to determine whether RA-058HM directly inhibits enzymes such as BACE1 or γ-secretase, stabilizes cytoskeletal dynamics, or exerts its effects primarily through antioxidant and antiinflammatory pathways.
Astrocytes play a crucial role in supporting synaptic function, and changes in astrocytic activity may underlie some of the therapeutic effects observed with RA-058HM.

The reduction in TNF-α levels in RA-058HM-treated mice is particularly significant, as TNF-α is known to upregulate BACE1, the enzyme responsible for Aβ production 7 60 Y. Furthermore, TNF-α reduction inhibits the activation of A1 astrocytes, a reactive and neurotoxic subtype, potentially shifting the astrocytic population towards the neuroprotective A2 phenotype (Liddelow et al. This shift could support synaptic resilience and contribute to the restoration of cognitive function observed in this study.

In summary, our study demonstrates that RA-058HM exerts multifaceted effects on Alzheimer’s disease pathology in the 5xFAD mouse model (Fig. We observed significant improvements in behavioural cognition, reduced amyloidogenesis, restored synaptic function, and decreased neuroinflammation (Fig. These effects suggest that RA-058HM not only targets amyloid pathology but also modulates neuroinflammatory responses and mitochondrial health, which are increasingly recognized as critical contributors to AD progression.

However, since AD is a complex, multifactorial disease with incompletely understood mechanisms, the exact pathways through which RA-058HM exerts these effects remain to be fully elucidated (Fig. While RA-058HM demonstrated significant effects on cognitive function, amyloid pathology, synaptic s, and… 761 transmission, mitochondrial dynamics, and neuroinflammation in the 5xFAD model, the precise molecular mechanism underlying these multifactorial therapeutic effects remains to be elucidated.

Future studies will be necessary to identify the primary receptor(s) or signaling pathways modulated by RA-058HM and to characterize its pharmacokinetic properties, which will be critical for advancing its development as a potential therapeutic for AD. Further studies are needed to confirm its effects in additional AD models, such as 3xTg- AD mice, and in aged wild-type animals, to ensure the generalizability of these results across different pathological and genetic contexts.

Although we observed significant anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects of RA-058HM following an 8-week administration period, it remains to be determined whether similar benefits can be achieved with shorter dosing intervals.
Future studies will be needed to evaluate the temporal dynamics of RA-058HM’s effects.

Long-term follow-up studies will be necessary to assess the durability of RA- 058HM’s cognitive benefits and to evaluate the safety profile of prolonged administration, which are critical steps toward its clinical development.

Notably, the effects of RA-058HM were more pronounced in the hippocampus than in the cortex, consistent with the earlier and more severe pathology typically observed in the hippocampus of 5xFAD mice at this stage of the disease.

These regional differences may reflect distinct neuropathological trajectories, suggesting that RA-058HM’s therapeutic impact may vary across brain regions—a finding that warrants further investigation in future studies.

Future studies employing human iPSC-derived neurons and glial cells will be essential to validate efficacy and elucidate the mechanism of RA-058HM in a human-relevant cellular context, strengthening its development as a potential therapeutic for AD. By targeting multiple aspects of AD pathology, RA- 058HM represents a promising candidate for AD therapy, potentially offering a more comprehensive approach than current single-target treatments.
Our findings provide a foundational framework for future investigations into the therapeutic potential of RA-058HM, which could 7 62 effects of RA-058HM in an AD mouse model.
In 5xFAD mice treated with RA-058HM, amyloid production was suppressed through the reduction of BACE1 levels in the brain.
Treatment also restored synaptic function and mitochondrial mobility while alleviating neuroinflammation.
Ultimately, these effects were associated with the recovery of cognitive function contribute to the development of novel, multi-targeted treatment strategies for Alzheimer’s disease.
